questions.question: Explain how crop farming and livestock farming contribute to soil erosion.
questions.expected_answer: Crop farming: clearing natural vegetation; ploughing breaks soil structure and leaves bare soil, especially after ploughing and after harvest; first spring storms; ploughing downslope channels runoff; monoculture lowers organic matter; cultivating steep or fragile land; removing windbreaks; machinery compacts soil; poor irrigation (erosion, salinity). Livestock: overgrazing beyond carrying capacity, loss of palatable grasses, trampling and compaction, animal paths become rills and dongas, worse in droughts. About 80% of SA agricultural land used mainly for grazing.

questions.question: Using the Dust Bowl and South African examples, explain how agriculture led to severe erosion.
questions.expected_answer: Dust Bowl: southern Great Plains (Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, New Mexico); prairie grass ploughed for wheat (WWI prices, tractors in 1920s); droughts from about 1930; wind erosion, black blizzards, Black Sunday 14 April 1935; dust reached the east coast; farms lost, dust pneumonia, mass migration; Soil Conservation Service 1935, windbreaks. SA: Karoo overgrazing by sheep and goats; former homelands (Transkei, Ciskei, KwaZulu) overcrowded due to Land Acts 1913/1936 (about 13% of land), cattle as wealth; betterment schemes imposed without consent caused resistance.

questions.question: Describe and explain soil conservation methods used by farmers.
questions.expected_answer: Keep soil covered, slow runoff, reduce wind. Contour ploughing; terraces; contour banks; strip cropping; conservation agriculture/no-till (no ploughing, permanent cover, crop rotation); windbreaks and standing stubble; stock within carrying capacity, rotational grazing, spread water points, fencing and replanting; gabions and brushwood in gullies, diverting water. SA: Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 1983; LandCare programme.
